rv.q: Ali Bianchi’s movement – with Greenwood bouncing about the set, powered by passion, ambition and later anxiety, distress and fear – keeps the action kinetically vital.
This is a fantastic play about the complexities of life, reminding us that human beings are not and never will be linear.
A thoroughly enjoyable and refreshingly different theatrical experience.
Greenwood's well-written, entertaining and frequently gripping play exploring the blindness of love is cleverer than that, offering parallels not certainties.
Relative Motion may not be the most original play about an abusive partner, but it does what it does well.
While the writing remains fairly unremarkable throughout, the dynamics in Greenwood’s story make it more interesting as they develop.
This is an accomplished play that raises questions while presenting an assured script and characters.

There’s a really interesting tale of how a relationship turns toxic here, and the central actors are deeply compelling, but the high-concept nature of the structure works against itself, rather than with it.
There is clear potential in the idea, with some powerful and unsettling moments, but at this point the production does not quite sustain the momentum needed to bring all the elements together.
But my feeling is that too much is crammed into too small a space — a bit like a typical tube journey.

The episodic structure works particularly well, with each encounter revealing another small shift in the balance of power and allowing the tension to build steadily. The performances are compelling. Sean Hart plays Paul with an unnerving elasticity, moving effortlessly between charm, vulnerability, resentment and aggression.

Relative Motion’s writing style, obvious and immediate, can feel a little jarring until the reality between the couple becomes clear, though there is still something deeply odd about Paul right from our first encounter, where everything feels just too good to be true.
I had a good time at Relative Motion, and I would happily see more from Greenwood as a writer.
Despite the contrivances, the two performances are grounded and brittle and director Wiebke Green keeps the production buzzing with dark energy.
Instead, the play occasionally feels caught between a conventional relationship drama and the more imaginative romantic comedy it has the potential to become.

cn.t: Critics find "Relative Motion" an ambitious, original concept—mapping coercive love through Newtonian physics—but execution divides opinion. Performances earn praise; the science-drama fusion feels strained to some, compelling to others.
